To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the surface tension of acids (and salts with strong ion surface interaction) can be described by a single parameter (adhesivity) and that it is a function of the bulk salt concentration, the surface tension of the pure solvent, and the surface tension of a saturated solution of the salt in the solvent.

(a) The nonlinear Poisson Boltzman theory of surface tension of acids and salts can be extended to include the effect of adhesivity, (b) The surface tension of acids is well described in the regime where the nonlinear Poisson Boltzmam theory is applicable and the adhesivity is weak, (c) The surface tension is well described in a wider regime of salt concentrations when adhesivity is strong,

(i) the surface tension of 2:1 salts and acids with strongly adsorbing ions is significantly affected by adhesivity; (ii) adhesivity can be quantified by fitting experimental data to the theoretical predictions; (iii) the theory is valid in the range of low salt concentrations and low adhesivity, where it is in agreement with experiments
In summary, our research is concerned with
the surface tension of electrolytes in the limit of high salt concentrations, where surface effects become important.
the calculation of the surface tension of 2D electrolytes, where ions interact with the interface with adhesivity.
the surface tension of 1:1 electrolytes, and the effects of adhesion of the ions to the interface.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for the systems studied, the surface tension of 1:1 electrolyte solutions is well described by the nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann theory for salt concentrations below 0.5 M.
the surface tension of acids (and salts), in general, is well described by the nonlinear Poisson Boltmann theory with a strong ion surface interaction.
the theory works well for most of the cases, and that the adhesivity parameters obtained are in good agreement with those obtained from the theory of adsorption of ions on solid surfaces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nonlinear Poisson Boltmann theory of surface tension, which includes adhesivity effects, is in excellent quantitative agreement with experimental data for a wide range of acids and salts.
our theory is able to describe accurately the experimental data on surface tension of 1:1 electrolytes, and that the theory can be extended to acids and salts with strong ion surface interaction.

, in the limit of strong adsorption, the surface tension of acid solutions is well described by the nonlinear Poisson Boltmann theory, whereas for weak adsorption the Onsager-Samaras theory gives a better description of the surface tension.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in general, the surface tension is not only a function of the bulk ionic concentration but also of the adhesivities of the ions.
the surface tension of acid (and salt) solutions can be described with high accuracy using the nonlinear Poisson Boltzman theory and the adhesivity model.

the nonlinear Poisson Boltzman equation, which is a mean field approximation of the Poisson Nernst Planck equation, provides a good description of the surface tension of acids and salts in the regime where the adsorption of the ionic species onto the interface is not too strong.
